story:
Honolulu's register of exceptional trees puts 26.5 metres around this banyan. That is not a trunk. It is the girth of a crowd of trunks, a tree that has spent its life setting down new legs, and the register's own diameter for it, 7.26 metres, describes something closer to a small building than a stem.

It stands at the Diamond Head corner of Kapiolani Park's archery range, on Poni Moi Road, just before the turning into La Pietra. The city assessed it in January 2017, rated its condition good and recorded a height of 23 metres. A 2025 City Council bill restating the protected list still names it at this corner, which is as close to a recent sighting as the paperwork gets.

Beyond the paperwork, almost nobody has written about it. No guidebook entry, no plaque, no planting story. Its one close rival stands about 200 metres away across Paki Avenue, at the tennis courts, and the register measures that one slightly wider.

An Indian banyan grows outward more than upward. Branches drop aerial roots, the roots thicken into new trunks, and over decades a single tree becomes a colonnade. Twenty-six metres of girth is what that looks like after a long time left alone.

Nobody has dated it, and the register has no column for age. If you know when it went in, tell us.

story:
The Waikiki War Memorial Natatorium is fenced and closed. The two banyans in front of it are still growing, and the inland one has a girth of 24 metres.

The city's register carries them as a pair, the mauka tree on the inland side and the makai tree towards the sea, and a 2025 City Council bill restating that list names both, in front of the memorial. The inland tree measures 24.1 metres round and stands 21.3 metres tall. Its seaward partner is 10.2 metres round and about 17.7 metres tall. The city rated both in good condition when it assessed them in January 2017.

Read those girths as the size of a crowd of trunks rather than a single one. The register's diameter figures for both trees do not match its circumferences, and the likeliest reading is that the tape went around the whole mass of stems and aerial roots, which is how an Indian banyan grows, setting down new legs from its branches until one tree becomes a colonnade.

One honest caution about getting close. The trees stand on the park-side frontage of the memorial, beside the beach walk from Kapiolani Park, but no published source says exactly where the memorial's fence runs. Expect to see them well from the walk, and treat standing under them as a bonus.

Nobody has dated either tree, and the register keeps no ages. If you know when they went in, tell us.

story:
This banyan is wider round than it is tall, by nearly six metres. Honolulu's exceptional trees register gives it a girth of 19.2 metres and a height of only 13.4, a tree that has spent its life building outward instead of up.

It is the seaward one of two banyans flanking the entrance to the Waikiki Shell parking lot, off Monsarrat Avenue. Its inland partner is the slimmer of the pair, 7.3 metres round and a little taller at 14.6 metres. The register lists them separately, a 2025 City Council bill restating the protected list names both at this entrance, and the city rated both in good condition when it assessed them in January 2017.

The Waikiki Shell is Honolulu's open-air concert stage, and plenty of the people who pass this tree are on their way in to a show. It deserves a look in daylight. The girth figure is not a single trunk but the whole spread of stems and rooted props a banyan sends down from its branches, and the register's own diameter for it disagrees with that girth, a sign of how hard these trees are to put a tape around.

The pin sits on the Shell itself and is approximate. At the lot entrance, pick the bigger tree on the sea side.

Nobody has published an age for either banyan. If you know when they went in, tell us.

story:
A walking guide written by tree people stops on the Kapiolani beach walk for what it calls an excellent Indian banyan, and this is very probably the tree it means. The guide, from the Outdoor Circle's Waikiki branch, puts the stop on the beach walk just before you cross Kalakaua Avenue to the banyans at the zoo gate. It gives no register number, so the match is likely rather than certain.

The register itself is plain about the tree. It stands on the Ewa side of the Queen's Surf Beach Center, on the sea side of Kalakaua Avenue, and a 2025 City Council bill restating Honolulu's protected list names it there. It measures 14.9 metres round and 17.7 metres tall, and the city rated it in good condition in January 2017. The register's diameter for it, 3.73 metres, works out to a smaller girth than the one it records, the usual gap when a banyan's measured mass includes props and secondary trunks as well as the main stem.

What it watches is the beach. Swimmers, the evening walk along the shore, the long line of Kapiolani Park's banyans running back towards Diamond Head. It is about 230 metres from the Zoo Gate banyans, which makes the two an easy pair on one stroll.

Nobody has dated it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

story:
Across the road from a public tennis centre stands a banyan that Honolulu's register measures at 27.4 metres round. Of the trees on this Oahu page, only the hula mound banyan at Kuhio Beach is recorded wider.

The register's own wording places it with unusual care. A 2025 City Council bill restating the protected list calls it the Ewa tree across the street from the Donald A. Andrews Diamond Head Tennis Center, along the makai side of Paki Avenue, which is the sea side, in Kapiolani Park. The city assessed it in January 2017, rated it in good condition, and recorded a height of 18.6 metres. Its girth runs about nine metres beyond its height.

That girth is a measure of a whole banyan, props and secondary trunks included, and the register's diameter for it, 3.38 metres, describes something far smaller, most likely the main stem alone. Both numbers can be true at once, which is the nature of a tree that keeps setting down new trunks from its branches.

A second banyan on the inland side of Paki Avenue is also on the register, but its figures contradict each other by a factor of four, so we leave them out until somebody measures it again.

This is the Diamond Head end of Kapiolani Park, a walk of about a kilometre from the Waikiki Shell, and the Poni Moi Road banyan is roughly 200 metres on. Nobody has dated either. If you know, tell us.

story:
When a protected earpod on Keeaumoku Street was cut down in November 2013, the kapok next to it was left standing. It is still here, on the grounds of the Hawaii Department of Agriculture at one of the busiest corners in town, King and Keeaumoku.

Honolulu Magazine called it the grandest canopy among the urban trees of that stretch when it profiled the city's exceptional trees in 2021, and put its age at roughly 130 years. The magazine gave no basis for that figure, so treat it as an estimate. If it holds, the tree was already old when the former Territorial Board of Agriculture building went up on these grounds in 1930.

The register's numbers are firm. It stands 22.9 metres tall, its trunk is 3.84 metres across and 12.07 metres round, and both measurements agree with each other, which is rarer on Honolulu's list than you would think. A 2025 City Council bill restating the protected list still names it, at this address.

It is not alone on the grounds. The same grounds hold two more exceptional trees, a mamee apple and a West Indian elm, which makes a government office lot one of the odder small arboretums on the island.

It is best seen from the S King Street pavement, since the grounds belong to a working state office. From there the crown is easy to pick out above the traffic.

story:
This is a fruit tree that stands taller than the banyans around it. Honolulu's exceptional trees register measures it at 20.1 metres, a height most people would never expect from a mango, and rates its condition excellent.

It stands by itself in the middle of a sloped lawn in Nuuanu Valley Park, to the right of the parking lot as you come in. Honolulu Magazine, profiling the city's protected trees in 2021, described exactly that scene, one tree with one picnic bench under its outer branches and nothing else competing for the slope. The magazine also noted that it produces a great deal of fruit, which is the other reason to look where you put your feet.

The trunk is 7.04 metres round and 2.24 metres across. A 2025 City Council bill restating the protected list still names it here.

The same park holds the Nuuanu Valley monkeypod, about 115 metres away, so the two make a short walk together. Nobody has published a planting date or an age for the mango, and girth alone will not give one. If you know when it went in, tell us.

story:
The whole North Shore of Oahu has one tree on Honolulu's exceptional list, according to Honolulu Magazine, and it shades a library car park. The magazine's 2021 survey of the city's protected trees found it here, its canopy spread over the lot between the Waialua Public Library and the gas station next door.

The same piece says it was planted in 1902. That is a single published claim with no source named, but if it holds, the tree is about 124 years old, and the magazine already counted it at nearly 120 in 2021.

The register measures it at 19.5 metres tall and 6.95 metres round, a trunk 2.21 metres across, and rates its condition excellent. A 2025 City Council bill restating the protected list still names it at this address.

An earpod takes its name from its seed pods, which curl round on themselves into the shape of an ear. It is a close relative of the monkeypod and often confused with it, which is why the pods are worth a look.

Waialua is about 40 kilometres from Waikiki, a drive rather than a walk, which suits a North Shore day. The library keeps its own hours, but the tree is in the lot and needs nobody's permission to see.

story:
At 34.1 metres, this is the tallest tree on this Oahu list, and its trunk looks as if somebody painted it. Honolulu's exceptional trees register measures it at 112 feet and rates it excellent, and the city's own self-guided tour of Wahiawa Botanical Garden puts it first, stop number one, before anything else in the collection.

The colour is the draw. The tour, from the city's Department of Parks and Recreation, says the young bark starts green and matures through to maroon, so a single trunk carries several stages at once. The tour calls the species by its other name, Mindanao gum, after the Philippine island.

The trunk is 1.32 metres across in the register, which works out to about 4.15 metres round, a modest figure next to all that height. Hawaii Magazine, writing about the garden in 2024, noted that rainbow eucalyptus give it shade, and that entry costs nothing. A 2025 City Council bill restating the protected list still names this tree.

Nobody has published a planting date, and on a species this fast-growing, size says little about age. If you know when it went in, tell us.

Wahiawa sits in the middle of the island, about 40 minutes by car from Honolulu, which makes it an easy stop on the way to the North Shore.

story:
This tree stands no taller than a three-storey building, and its trunk is more than four metres round. Honolulu's Exceptional Trees register gives it a girth of 426.7 centimetres and a height of just 9.4 metres, which makes the banuyo by Sinclair Library a tree built wide rather than up. The register rates its vitality good.

Banuyo is a rarity in its own right. Wallaceodendron celebicum is a legume tree from Sulawesi, the island once called Celebes that gives it its Latin name, and from the Philippines. Its genus is named after the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, who collected in those islands in the 1850s. It is not a tree you pass on many street corners, in Hawaii or anywhere else.

The city protects it by ordinance. A 2025 Honolulu bill listing the island's exceptional trees places it on the University of Hawaii at Manoa campus, along Campus Road near Sinclair Library, across from Gartley Hall. The campus is open on foot and there is no ticket.

On its own it is a short detour. It earns its place as part of a walk, because the Sinclair cannonball tree, the Art Building baobab and the skunk tree by George Hall all stand within a few hundred metres, so four of the register's stranger trees fit in one loop.

Nobody has published its age or when it was planted. If you know, tell us.
